condition: Hypertensive urgency — severely elevated blood pressure (186/102) with headache following an amlodipine dose increase, without documented evidence of acute end-organ damage; risk of progression to hypertensive emergency is increased by the missed 1800 monitoring check
evaluationParameters: Blood pressure trend: manual recheck within 15-30 minutes and then per order/provider direction, evaluating for SBP reduction toward < 180 without an abrupt drop (avoid > 25% reduction in the first hour) and without symptomatic hypotension

Neurologic and end-organ symptom status: headache severity on a 0-10 scale, level of consciousness, vision changes, focal deficits, chest pain, dyspnea, and urine output, evaluated for resolution versus escalation to hypertensive emergency
missingInformation: Baseline and prior BP values for Mrs. Vega, including all readings since admission and the reading that would have been obtained at 1800
Complete current vital signs: heart rate, respiratory rate, temperature, SpO2, and BP in both arms with documented cuff size and patient position
Focused neurologic assessment findings: pupils, orientation, motor/sensory symmetry, visual changes, and whether the headache is new, sudden-onset, or worst-ever
Headache characteristics: onset time, quality, location, severity score, aggravating factors, and response to any analgesia already given
Whether the increased amlodipine dose was actually administered today, the exact time, the old and new dose, and any other scheduled or PRN antihypertensives on the MAR
Presence of any PRN or standing antihypertensive order the nurse may act on before the provider returns the call
Relevant history: hypertension control at home, home antihypertensive regimen and last doses taken, stroke/CAD/CKD/heart failure history, pregnancy status, and admitting diagnosis
Associated symptoms: chest pain, dyspnea, nausea/vomiting, epistaxis, edema, or anxiety/pain that could be transiently elevating BP
Recent laboratory and diagnostic data: creatinine/BUN, electrolytes, troponin, ECG, and any imaging
Documentation of the handoff itself — what was communicated, by whom, and to whom — for incident reporting and unit follow-up
priorityActions: Immediately recheck the BP manually with a correctly sized cuff with Mrs. Vega resting and seated/supine, while performing a rapid focused assessment for end-organ involvement (level of consciousness, vision changes, focal neuro deficits, chest pain, dyspnea) and obtaining full vital signs

Notify the hospitalist without delay per the ordered call parameter (SBP > 180), using SBAR to report the 186/102 reading, the headache, the amlodipine dose increase today, and the missed 1800 check, and request orders for BP management and monitoring frequency
reasoning: The stem supplies a single objective abnormality — BP 186/102 — paired with headache, a classic symptom of markedly elevated pressure, in a patient whose amlodipine dose was increased the same day. Severe hypertension with a symptom but no stated evidence of acute target-organ injury is best labeled hypertensive urgency; hypertensive emergency cannot be excluded from the stem because no neurologic, cardiac, or renal assessment data are given, which is why the first priority action pairs BP verification with a focused end-organ assessment. Verification also guards against a spurious reading from cuff size, position, or activity. The second priority action is dictated explicitly by the stem: the hospitalist wrote a call parameter for SBP > 180, and 186 breaches it, so notification is a non-discretionary nursing obligation; the report must include the amlodipine change and the missed 1800 check because both alter clinical interpretation — the dose change means a pharmacologic effect may still be developing, and the missed check means the current value has no recent trend to anchor it. Evaluation parameters follow directly from the two actions: serial BP to judge whether the pressure is responding and to guard against an overly rapid drop, and serial neurologic/end-organ symptom assessment to detect conversion to hypertensive emergency. Confidence is medium rather than high because the stem gives one BP, one symptom, and no assessment findings, so the urgency-versus-emergency distinction rests on absent rather than negative data. The incomplete, dismissive handoff is a contributing system factor and a documentation/reporting issue rather than a nursing priority ahead of patient assessment and provider notification.
